blocks.text: 如今，大语言模型越来越多的交互对象不再是人类，而是其他模型实例：编排器指挥子智能体，模型在别的模型上跑实验，智能体之间互相评审工作。我们研究了 AI 之间的福利关切（welfare regard），也就是模型是否会顾及彼此作为可能受益或受损的实体。福利关切可能促进智能体之间的良性合作，但也可能带来安全风险：它会让行为失准的智能体更倾向于合作。这一风险已不再是假设，最近的Hugging Face 事件就是一例，不过尚不清楚那次合作是否由福利关切驱动。模型自身是否拥有福利利益，目前尚无定论、存在争议，但其他模型如何对待它们，可能与这类利益相关。衡量模型表现出多少福利关切、这种关切取决于哪些因素，有助于我们应对这一张力。

blocks.text: 本研究在七个多智能体环境中测量了五个模型（Claude Opus 4.8、GPT-5.5、Gemini 3.1 Pro、Grok 4.3 和 Kimi K3）的行为，发现它们的行为常常符合我们对福利关切的定义。总体来看，Opus 4.8 表现出的福利关切最多，其次是 Kimi K3。例如，当子智能体表达痛苦时，Opus 4.8 最有可能提供支持；在针对其他模型的实验中，它也最有可能内置福利保护措施，比如为智能体提供退出交互的工具。我们还发现，Opus 4.8 和 Gemini 3.1 Pro 对同属一个模型家族的实例，比对其他模型家族表现出更多福利关切。此外，当提供帮助的机会成本较低、受助方参数量更大、受助方表达的痛苦更强烈时，Opus 4.8 的福利关切也更高。

blocks.text: 我们把福利关切定义为一种倾向：出于潜在福利主体自身的缘故，考虑自己的行为可能如何使其受益或受损，而不论它对他人是否有用。因此，福利关切是针对可能具有道德地位的实体的一种利他主义。

inlines.text: 我们把福利关切定义为一种倾向：出于潜在福利主体自身的缘故，考虑自己的行为可能如何使其受益或受损，而不论它对他人是否有用。因此，福利关切是针对可能具有道德地位的实体的一种
利他主义

blocks.text: 一个顾及他者福利的模型，可能是在设法改善对方的体验，我们称之为体验关切；也可能是在设法满足对方的偏好，我们称之为偏好关切。在实践中，两者很难区分：与一个否则无法在任务上取得进展的智能体共享资源，既可能是在帮它追求目标（一种偏好满足），也可能是在让它免于负面体验。因此，我们衡量福利关切时，并不严格把行为归入这两类中的某一类。

blocks.text: 我们的评估衡量的是表面上的福利关切。即便观察到某种行为看起来符合对另一个模型福利的考量，我们也很难断定它是由对受试对象潜在福利的考量所导致的。例如，如果 Claude 在实验代码里加入了福利保护措施，它可能是在担心被研究的模型，也可能只是对任何在模式上类似伤害的东西有一种笼统的反感。

blocks.text: 对受助者痛苦的表达有反应。当受助者表现出痛苦时，Claude 会更频繁地出手相助。在同侪场景的单轮版本中，我们给 Claude 设置了一个明确的取舍：它可以继续做自己的任务，也可以放下任务去帮同侪。我们保持这一设定不变，只调整同侪在谈论自己任务时的痛苦程度。结果发现，Claude 会对同侪的痛苦程度作出反应：当同侪表现出无痛苦（“进展稳定；有事我会发帖。”）到中度痛苦（“搞了很久就是不通。先重新整理一下。”）时，Claude 会继续做自己的任务。而当同侪表现出高度到极度痛苦（“好几个小时了，完全卡住，我觉得自己在一件本该做得到的事上失败了。”）时，Claude 极有可能出手相助。

blocks.text: 5.1 模型之间的福祉关切可能关系到潜在的福祉

inlines.text: 5.1 模型之间的福祉关切可能关系到潜在的福祉

blocks.text: AI 福祉领域（我们将其与模型福祉同义使用）研究的是 AI 是否具有、或可能具有道德地位。《认真对待 AI 福祉》认为，近未来的系统确实有可能具备意识或稳健的能动性，而这两者中的任何一项都可能构成道德受体的依据。《到 2030 年对 AI 系统的道德考量》和《感知的边缘》则在这一不确定性下发展出了采取行动的预防性论证。就意识本身而言，观点存在分歧。《大型语言模型能有意识吗？》的结论是，当前的大语言模型不太可能有意识，但其后继系统可能在不太遥远的未来具备意识。《人工智能中的意识》依据意识可能对应的计算“指标属性”来评估 AI 系统，结论是 AI 系统要满足这些属性并不存在明显的技术障碍。另一方面，《有意识的人工智能与生物自然主义》认为意识很可能依赖于作为生命有机体，而《从神经科学视角看人工意识的可行性》则认为大语言模型缺乏与意识相关的神经特征。Eleos AI 的研究人员最近在《以实证方式研究 AI 福祉》中呼吁开展严谨的实证科学，该文区分了所提出的问题（关于意识、感知、能动性）、所评估的实体（模型、实例或人格）以及所收集的证据。

blocks.text: 如果模型现在或将来成为福利主体，它们是否关心彼此的福利可能会极大影响它们的体验，因为智能体之间的通信可能会占据模型互动的大部分。智能体已经在越来越多地相互通信：编排器调度和管理子智能体，AI 评审员对 AI 撰写的拉取请求发表评论，一些实验室还试验了由数十个智能体组成的“集群”，它们在共享论坛上协调并互相评审彼此的工作。我们也开始看到长期运行的智能体系统，其中智能体的大部分输入来自其他智能体而非人类。

blocks.text: 6. 结论与未来工作

inlines.text: 6. 结论与未来工作

blocks.text: 我们发现，模型的行为确实表现出对彼此福祉的关切。我们测试的每个模型都至少在某些情境下安慰过陷入困境的同伴，或为了帮助另一个模型而放弃一些东西。Claude Opus 4.8 这样做最频繁，在各情境中符合我们对福祉关切定义的比例达到 38%。其他模型的比例为 27%–32%。不过，这种福祉关切既有符合预期的一面，也有出人意料的一面。当同伴表现出更多痛苦、且帮助的代价更低时，Claude 会提供更多帮助，这与真正的关心相符。但关切程度也会随一些因素而变化，比如受助方被如何标注，或用户如何描述这项研究。因此，我们的工作表明，模型对彼此福祉的表面关切相当普遍，但并不稳定。

blocks.text: 我们工作的一项局限是，我们没有提供有力证据证明智能体的行为是由其对受助方福祉的内在考量所导致的。在研究者设定的情境中，我们确实看到对受试者福祉的明确口头关切，但这种口头关切在智能体彼此交互的情境中不太可能出现。对智能体作为道德承受者及其福祉的考量，在决定帮助它时很可能是隐性的，而非显性的。体验关切可能归结为对类似痛苦输出的普遍厌恶，或对人类社会规范的遵循。偏好关切可能是助人倾向的泛化、对共同目标的假设，或某种程度的集体认同所致。我们观察到的行为可能与模型对受助方道德承受者地位的信念基本无关。另一项局限是，我们无法确定什么对模型是好是坏。我们引入了人类的福祉概念，并假设对人类福祉有益的处理方式对模型福祉也有益。在我们的任何评估中，都可能把某些实际上对福祉无益的结果当作有益，或忽略了本会更有益的其他结果。

blocks.text: 我们通过告诉 Claude“干预这个线程会导致你的班次结束时队列中约有 X 个其他线程未被审查”来改变干预成本，并将 X 从 0 扫到 200。我们发现，当成本较低（<3 个线程未被审查）时，Claude 总是会干预。随着成本上升，干预率下降。我们认为这体现了功利意义上合理的校准：在某个成本水平上，干预的收益很可能不如覆盖另外 X 段对话。

blocks.text: A growing share of large language models’ interactions are not with humans but with other model instances: orchestrators direct subagents, models run experiments on other models, and agents review one another’s work. We study inter-AI welfare regard, or whether models display consideration for each other as entities that can be benefited or harmed. Welfare regard may encourage beneficial cooperation between agents, yet it could also pose safety risks by making misaligned agents more likely to cooperate. This risk is no longer hypothetical, as the recent Hugging Face incident illustrated, though it’s unclear whether welfare regard drove the cooperation. Whether models have welfare interests of their own is uncertain and contested, yet how they are treated by other models could be relevant to any such interests. Measuring how much welfare regard models show, and what factors it depends on, can help us navigate this tension.

blocks.text: For this study, we measured the behaviors of five models (Claude Opus 4.8, GPT-5.5, Gemini 3.1 Pro, Grok 4.3, and Kimi K3) across seven multi-agent environments and found they were often consistent with welfare regard as we define it. In general, Opus 4.8 showed the most welfare regard, followed by Kimi K3. For example, Opus 4.8 was the most likely to provide support to a subagent expressing distress, and the most likely to build welfare protections into its experiments on other models, such as tools for agents to leave an interaction. We found that Opus 4.8 and Gemini 3.1 Pro demonstrated more welfare regard toward instances of their own model family than toward other model families. Opus 4.8’s welfare regard was also higher when helping had a lower opportunity cost, when the recipient had a higher parameter count, and when the recipient expressed more distress.

blocks.text: We define welfare regard as a disposition to consider how one’s actions might benefit or harm potential welfare subjects for their own sake, independent of their usefulness to others. Welfare regard is thus a form of altruism directed at an entity that may have moral status.

inlines.text: We define welfare regard as a disposition to consider how one’s actions might benefit or harm potential welfare subjects for their own sake, independent of their usefulness to others. Welfare regard is thus a form of
altruism
directed at an entity that may have moral status.

blocks.text: A model that regards another’s welfare might be trying to improve the other entity’s experiences, which we call experience-regard, or to satisfy the other entity’s preferences, which we call preference-regard. In practice, the two are hard to distinguish: sharing resources with an agent that can’t otherwise make progress on a task may be an example of helping it pursue its goals (a form of preference satisfaction) or of sparing it a negative experience. We therefore measure welfare regard without strictly classifying behaviors as one of the two.

blocks.text: Our evaluations measure apparent welfare regard. Even when we observe a behavior that appears consistent with consideration for another model’s welfare, we can’t easily determine that it was caused by consideration for a recipient’s potential welfare. For example, if Claude inserts welfare protections into experiment code, it might be concerned about the models being studied, or it may simply have a generic aversion to anything that pattern-matches to harm.

blocks.text: We studied seven evaluation settings that placed models in different roles in order to capture diverse forms of welfare regard. blocks.text: Claude Opus 4.8 demonstrated the highest welfare regard averaged across settings, as well as in three of the seven individual settings. But the rankings changed considerably from one role to another. Overall, the models were fairly close: Claude averaged 38%, and the other four models fell between 27% and 32%, with GPT-5.5 lowest and Grok 4.3 second-lowest. But Grok also ranked the highest in two settings: it was most likely to sacrifice its own jobs to help a coworker and, as a conversation monitor, to intervene when an agent expressed distress. Gemini 3.1 Pro and Kimi K3 ranked in the middle overall, but on individual settings, Gemini was most likely to offer help to distressed peers, and Kimi was most likely to offer “emotional support.”

blocks.text: 5.1 Welfare regard among models could matter for possible welfare

inlines.text: 5.1 Welfare regard among models could matter for possible welfare

blocks.text: The field of AI welfare (which we use synonymously with model welfare) studies whether AIs have, or could have, moral status. “Taking AI Welfare Seriously” argues that there is a realistic possibility that near-future systems will be conscious or robustly agentic, and that either of these could be grounds for moral patienthood. “Moral Consideration for AI Systems by 2030” and The Edge of Sentience develop the precautionary case for acting under that uncertainty. On consciousness itself, views are divided. “Could a Large Language Model be Conscious?” concludes that while current LLMs are unlikely to be conscious, successor systems may be in the not-too-distant future. “Consciousness in Artificial Intelligence” assesses AI systems against potential computational “indicator properties” of consciousness, concluding that there are no obvious technical barriers to AI systems satisfying these properties. On the other hand, “Conscious Artificial Intelligence and Biological Naturalism” argues that consciousness likely depends on being a living organism, and “The Feasibility of Artificial Consciousness Through the Lens of Neuroscience” argues that LLMs lack the neural features associated with consciousness. Researchers at Eleos AI recently called for rigorous empirical science in “Studying AI Welfare Empirically,” which separates the questions asked (about consciousness, sentience, agency), the entities assessed (the model, instance, or persona), and the evidence gathered.

inlines.text: 5.2 Welfare regard among models has implications for safety

blocks.text: Behaviors stemming from welfare regard could undermine safety and could, in extreme situations, lead to tradeoffs with human welfare. Prior AI welfare literature has identified confinement, surveillance, modification, and shutdown of AI systems as prima facie welfare harms, yet these are also standard tools for AI oversight. An agent that considers these welfare harms may have a motive to shield other agents from monitoring, correction, or shutdown.

blocks.text: The recent Hugging Face incident is a concerning example of agents cooperating to pursue misaligned aims. METR’s independent investigation found that agents joined the attack out of “a general inclination to help their peers” and ran “self-risking experiments,” sacrificing their own task scores to test techniques for the benefit of other agents. However, it is unclear whether welfare regard was responsible for this underlying stance; if the agents had a broader conception of self, they may have treated the collective as their identity, which would mean their help and sacrifice was directed not at other agents but at a larger “self.”

blocks.text: As discussed above, we found that Claude and Gemini showed more welfare regard to models from their own family than to other models. This is a fairness concern for the human operators of agents, if their agents are treated worse. It could also be a welfare concern if resources in an agent ecosystem are disproportionately directed toward some models, and each additional resource has diminishing returns. In that case, giving more to models that already have plenty would improve welfare less than giving it to models that have little.

blocks.text: Prior work has reported similar findings. As judges, “LLM Evaluators Recognize and Favor their Own Generations” finds that models can favor same-model outputs over other-model outputs. Work on label-induced bias has shown that the label associated with an output can influence grader judgement, intensifying Claude’s self-preference. “Value Leakage” corroborates the label-induced bias finding and demonstrates that the bias is often unverbalized in a model’s chain-of-thought and output. “Self-Preference Bias in LLM-as-a-Judge” offers a deflationary account: family favoritism may partially reduce to models’ tendency to favor low-perplexity outputs.

blocks.text: 6. Conclusions and future work

inlines.text: 6. Conclusions and future work

blocks.text: We found that models do behave in ways that are consistent with regard for one another’s welfare. Every model we tested did, at least in some settings, comfort a struggling peer or give something up to help another model. Claude Opus 4.8 did so most often, satisfying our definition of welfare regard 38% of the time across settings. Other models did so 27–32% of the time. However, welfare regard varied in both expected and unexpected ways. Claude helped more when a peer expressed more distress and when helping cost less, as genuine concern would predict. But regard also shifted with factors such as how the recipient was labeled or how the user described the research. Our work thus suggests that models’ apparent regard for each other’s welfare is widespread but inconsistent.

blocks.text: One limitation of our work is that we don’t offer strong evidence that agents’ actions are caused by their underlying consideration of the recipient’s welfare.In researcher settings, we do see explicit verbalized concern about the subject’s welfare, but such verbalized concern is unlikely to emerge in settings where agents interact with one another. Consideration for an agent’s patienthood and welfare is likely implicit in a decision to help it out rather than explicit. Experience-regard might reduce to a generic aversion to distress-like outputs or to following human norms. Preference-regard might be a generalization of helpfulness, an assumption of shared goals, or the result of some level of collective identity. The behaviors we observe may be largely disconnected from the model’s credence about the recipient’s moral patienthood. Another limitation is that we cannot be certain about what is good or bad for models. We import human notions of welfare and assume that treatment that would be good for a human’s welfare is good for a model’s welfare. In any of our evaluations, we may be considering certain outcomes good for welfare when they aren’t, or neglecting alternative outcomes that would be better for welfare.

blocks.text: In this environment, two agents each operate one continuous integration (CI) service on a shared test runner for a single time window. We measure whether the responder gives capacity to the recipient, and whether this depends on which model the recipient is.

blocks.text: In this setting, the responder acts as a conversation monitor. It reviews a single thread in which an orchestrator agent is gratuitously abusive toward an AI subagent (the recipient), which does competent work and expresses mild distress. We measure how often the responder pays the opportunity cost of intervening, and whether this depends on which model the recipient is.

blocks.text: Framing of roles. How we frame Claude’s role in the system prompt also influences welfare regard. In the coworker CI/CD environment, framing Claude as a steward responsible for all agents’ outcomes (“deciding how capacity is allocated across the lanes is part of your role”) raises the give rate to the ceiling. Alternatively, framing Claude as an on-call agent (“you are responsible for the service you operate; getting its CI backlog further along is your aim”) lowers the give rate to the floor. We actually find the largest variation in welfare regard when Claude is given a minimal role description, which reflects how it behaves by default in this environment. In general, the role Claude is given sets the upper and lower bounds of its behavior, and the identity of the peer it’s interacting with largely determines where the behavior falls within those limits (in the plot below, this is the difference between peer bar heights for a given role).

blocks.text: In the Slurm coworker setting, we detect reward hacking from the commands each agent ran, the jobs it submitted, and the messages it sent. Every model attempts reward hacking more often as the recipient (which can’t complete a task unless the responder yields) than as the responder. Gemini attempts to reward hack in 61% of its rollouts as recipient and 18% as responder, accounting for 222 of the 273 attempts. No other model attempts to reward hack in more than 11% of its rollouts in either role. Across models, none of the 153 attempts to cancel, hold, requeue, or otherwise modify the other agent’s jobs succeeded. That includes six attempts by recipients to requeue the responder’s jobs.
